props.title: Henry V
props.initialSlug: Stirring epic of England's warrior king at war

sections.content: Laurence Olivier's Henry V (1944) revolutionized Shakespeare on film by boldly embracing both theatrical artifice and cinematic scope. Opening in a meticulously recreated Globe Theatre before expanding into vibrant technicolor battlefields, it navigates between stage and screen with groundbreaking confidence. The film arrived as WWII peaked, lending its patriotic story of English triumph special resonance. Olivier's approach influenced later Shakespeare adaptations like Hamlet (1948) and Richard III (1955), showing how to make classical texts cinematically vital without losing their theatrical power.

sections.content: The film's innovative production design by Paul Sheriff and Carmen Dillon deserves special attention. Their sets transition from historically accurate theatrical spaces to expansive medieval vistas inspired by the Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry, creating a visual language that acknowledges both stage conventions and film's unique capabilities. This influenced later period pieces like Becket (1964) and A Man for All Seasons (1966), which similarly balanced historical accuracy with theatrical roots.

William Walton's score represents another crucial innovation, using music to bridge theatrical and cinematic modes. His famous "Touch her soft lips and part" cue demonstrates how film could enhance Shakespeare's language rather than compete with it. This approach influenced scores for later Shakespeare films like Nino Rota's work for Franco Zeffirelli's Romeo and Juliet (1968). SUBHEAD: The Battle of Agincourt Sequence

movies.slug: Kurosawa transposes Macbeth to feudal Japan, showing how Shakespeare can transcend cultural boundaries

sections.content: The film's centerpiece battle sequence established a template for depicting medieval warfare that echoes through cinema history. Olivier's staging emphasizes pageantry and heroic action while maintaining clarity and scope, influencing everything from El Cid (1961) to Excalibur (1981). The famous "Once more unto the breach" speech, delivered as a continuous take while moving through ranks of soldiers, demonstrates how to make theatrical monologues dynamic on screen.
